source: Soar Manual (current), ch. 4 Procedural Knowledge Learning
finding: Chunking builds a new rule from the substate work that led to a result in the superstate. The chunk is built at once when the result is created, not when the impasse ends. Next time it fires in one step and no substate is needed.
numbers: Manual states hundreds of rule firings can compress to one. Learning is off by default.
quote: In future similar situations, the new chunk will fire and create the appropriate results in a single step
limits: Speed-up and transfer claims are design statements, not an experiment. Procedural learning is disabled by default.
agent_relevance: Maps to S6 plus the subgoal library: store the result of a resolved impasse with its trigger so the impasse does not recur. Compile at result time, not at the end.

source: Soar Manual ch. 4: Explanation-based behavior summarization (EBBS)
finding: Soar 9.6 replaced older chunking with EBBS because old chunks were over-specialized. EBBS makes rules far more general using identity-based variablization and constraint tracking.
numbers: Arithmetic agent: 1263 learned rules in Soar 9.4 versus 8 rules in Soar 9.6.
limits: One agent and one task, reported by the Soar team itself. No error rate for the general rules is given here.
agent_relevance: Warns that stored subgoal results can be too specific (never reused) or too general (wrong). Our library needs generalization with recorded conditions.

source: Soar Manual ch. 4: correctness, over-general rules and ROSK
finding: A chunk is correct if rerunning the substate would give the same result. Over-general rules are incorrect rules. Soar tracks relevant operator selection knowledge (ROSK) so the chunk includes the preferences that chose the operator, else it would not match the real processing.
numbers: No numbers. Definitions only.
limits: Manual also lists situations where a chunk is not learned and settings to prohibit known sources of correctness problems.
agent_relevance: Gives a direct stale-chunk test: replay the substate and compare the result. For our agent, a stored subgoal should be re-verified by running its check, not trusted.

source: Soar Manual ch. 4: bottom-up chunking
finding: When a result passes through several nested substates, one result can yield several chunks, one per level. Chunking stops when a chunk only writes into the state it matched in.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Describes the mechanism only.
agent_relevance: A nested subgoal library should store a skill at each level of decomposition, not only the top one.

source: Wray, Kirk, Laird (2021) Language Models as a Knowledge Source for Cognitive Agents
finding: Early Soar-group analysis of using LMs as a task knowledge source. Proposes template prompts for specific knowledge gaps and agent-side verification, and says the agent should learn an abstract model of what the LM knows.
numbers: Mentions COMET agreement with human raters above 90% as background; no new experiment.
limits: Position paper, no agent results.
agent_relevance: Impasse as a typed gap gives a narrow, targeted query to the model. Matches our rule that the program decides and the model fills a slot.

source: Kirk, Wray, Lindes, Laird (2023) Integrating Diverse Knowledge Sources for Online One-shot Learning of Novel Tasks
finding: A Soar task-learning agent combines environment search, human instruction and GPT-3 answers. Search results are turned into rules by chunking, so the agent does not search again on a similar task.
numbers: Kitchen tidy task, 35 goal assertions. Fully learned in one shot in every condition except Search+LLM, where only 54% of subtasks were completed. 30-40% of GPT-3 goal responses accepted by the human. GPT-3 gave 96% correct actions on first try but weak goals. LLM cut instructor words by about 50%. Instruction+search+LLM reached 100% completion.
quote: A side-effect of search in Soar is that control knowledge is learned via Soar's chunking mechanism
limits: Simulated robot, single task, text-davinci-002 (temperature 0). LLM errors included closing a bin with no lid and putting a dirty mug in a cupboard. The authors say LLMs are not reliable enough alone.
agent_relevance: Direct precedent: LLM answers are proposals that need verification before they are compiled. Search plus chunking removed repeat cost; the LLM only cut human effort.

source: Kirk, Wray, Laird (2023) Exploiting Language Models as a Source of Knowledge for Cognitive Agents
finding: The Soar agent prompts an LLM for a specific gap, verifies each response, then tries it and reviews the steps ('retrospection'). Chunking compiles the review into procedural knowledge so the LLM is not needed again.
numbers: Over 70% of LLM responses were not viable for the embodied agent. Planning (look-ahead) can virtually eliminate the need to ask the human, per early results (Kirk et al. 2023).
limits: Position paper with a summary chart. The full pipeline was not evaluated at scale ('remains future work').
agent_relevance: Supports a gated pipeline: model proposal, then code or environment check, then compile. Do not store an unverified proposal. Expect most raw proposals to fail.

source: Hu, Wang, Yang, Wang (2025) CogRec: A Cognitive Recommender Agent Fusing LLMs and Soar
finding: Soar runs the recommendation cycle. When it reaches a tie impasse it sends a structured query (context, impasse reason, task) to an LLM. The answer is parsed into a condition-action chunk that Soar compiles into a new rule.
numbers: Three datasets (ML-1M, Movies, Yelp). Paper reports CogRec above all baselines on HR@10/20 and NDCG@10/20. The ablation figure (not machine-readable here) shows removing LLM bootstrap hurts most, removing chunking falls toward LLM-Direct, and LLM call frequency falls over interactions with chunking but stays high without it.
quote: Upon encountering an impasse, it dynamically queries the LLM to obtain a reasoned solution.
limits: The extracted results table is garbled so exact scores were not read. The paper's own text claims significance. No independent replication. Datasets are recommendation, not problem solving.
agent_relevance: The only found system that implements the exact loop impasse -> LLM -> chunk -> fewer LLM calls, and it measures the call-frequency drop. A good model for a call-cost metric in our subgoal library.

source: Hu et al. (2025) CogRec learning-curve ablation: LLM Call Frequency (LCF)
finding: With chunking on, how often the agent calls the LLM drops and settles on a low plateau as interactions grow. With chunking off the call rate stays high because the agent must re-ask for every similar case.
numbers: Described from Figure 4 text; no numeric values extractable. Three ablations: w/o LLM-Bootstrap, w/o Chunking, w/o Soar.
limits: Figure values not read. Single research group.
agent_relevance: Gives the shape to expect and to test: calls per task should fall after the subgoal library fills. If it stays flat, compilation is not working.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) NL2GenSym: Natural Language to Generative Symbolic Rules for SOAR via LLMs
finding: LLM writes Soar rules from natural language. Rules are run in Soar. A critic LLM reads the execution trace and drives repair. Success rate on the Water Jug problem set was much higher than one-shot prompting.
numbers: 100 cases. Zero-shot SR 0 for both models. One-shot: Gemini-2.5-Pro 55%, Qwen-max 66%. NL2GenSym: 86% (Gemini-Flash) and 91% (Qwen). Hard cases: one-shot 20% vs 76.67% (Gemini) and 46.67% vs 86.67% (Qwen).
limits: Single domain (water jug). Models partly different between arms (Pro baseline vs Flash framework). Authors' own dataset.
agent_relevance: Execution-grounded critic is the key piece: ablating the critic cut SR by 23% overall. Same as our G2: revise from real output.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) NL2GenSym efficiency and ablation
finding: Generated rules also solve faster. Average decision cycles fell from thousands of times optimal (manual) to about 2 times optimal. Removing parts of the framework hurt.
numbers: Manual rules: ~3390x the minimum decision cycles overall. NL2GenSym: 1.76x (Flash) and 1.98x (Qwen). Ablation: no critic -23% SR (37% on hard/variant); no basic knowledge base -17%; no case base -14%. Flash with framework (86% SR) beat Pro one-shot (55%).
limits: Compute limit of 500,000 cycles ends hard manual cases. Water jug only.
agent_relevance: A small model with an execution-checked rule loop beat a larger model prompted plainly. Supports G7 only if we measure at equal tokens.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) NL2GenSym appendix: Soar impasse types in generated agent
finding: The critic's advice list shows a real failure: a 'state no-change' impasse produced an infinite loop. It told the generator to detect and handle all impasse types: state no-change, operator no-change, tie, conflict, constraint-failure.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Appendix example, not a measured effect.
agent_relevance: A budget stop on repeated no-change states is needed in any impasse detector, matching G6/G7 and our loop guards.

source: Prasad et al. (2024) ADaPT: As-Needed Decomposition and Planning with Language Models
finding: The agent tries a task. Only if the executor fails does a planner split it into subtasks, recursively up to a depth limit. This is impasse-driven subgoaling with no learning step.
numbers: GPT-3.5. ALFWorld overall: ADaPT 71.6 vs ReAct 43.3, Plan-and-Execute 43.3, Try Again 47.8, Reflexion 57.5. WebShop: 44.0 vs ReAct 32.0, Reflexion 35.0, LATS 38.0. TextCraft: 52.0 vs ReAct 19.0, Plan-and-Execute 27.0, Reflexion 32.0. Max depth 3 (4 for TextCraft).
limits: Single base model for headline numbers; text-only benchmarks. Prompts tuned per dataset.
agent_relevance: Closest published LLM analogue of S6: decompose when the attempt fails, not on a schedule (G1). Gains over Plan-and-Execute isolate the value of as-needed splitting.

source: Prasad et al. (2024) ADaPT: depth and executor-capability analysis
finding: Adaptive decomposition depth adjusts to model strength and task difficulty. Compared with Reflexion, which reruns the whole task, ADaPT retries only the failed subtask.
numbers: ALFWorld per-type: Pick2 task 52.9 vs 5.9 for Reflexion and ReAct 11.8. ADaPT improves ReAct by 28.3 points absolute, Plan-and-Execute by 28.3 and Try Again by 23.8.
limits: Does not store the decomposition for later tasks, so there is no chunking analogue.
agent_relevance: Shows the missing half: ADaPT has trigger and substate but no compile step. Adding a cache of solved subtasks would be our untested extension.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: After a failed trial the agent writes a verbal lesson and keeps it in episodic memory for the next trial. It is whole-trial learning, not scoped to a subgoal.
numbers: ALFWorld: ReAct+Reflexion completed 130 of 134 tasks in 12 trials, +22% absolute over baselines. HotPotQA +20%, HumanEval pass@1 91% vs 80% GPT-4. ReAct-only plateaued between trials 6 and 7.
limits: Needs a failure signal and repeated trials on the same task. ADaPT paper notes it re-executes steps that already worked. Hallucination detection heuristic used.
agent_relevance: Lessons are stored without the conditions that make them safe to reuse (the 2026 review's point). Our subgoal record should carry its trigger and a re-check.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Agent induces reusable workflows (named routines with steps) from past successful runs and gives selected ones to later tasks. This is a chunk-like compiled routine from experience, learned offline or online.
numbers: Relative success gain +24.6% on Mind2Web and +51.1% on WebArena; WebArena success 35.5% vs BrowserGym 23.5% (12.0 points absolute); about 2.0 fewer steps per success than a baseline and 40.8 fewer than another. Online AWM gap over baselines grows from 8.9 to 14.0 points as train-test distance widens.
limits: Learns from successes, not from impasses. No stale-routine check reported. GPT-4 at temperature 0 in main runs.
agent_relevance: Evidence that compiled routines raise success and cut steps in LLM agents. Our library differs by keying entries to the impasse that created them.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) AgentDebugX: Failure Observability, Attribution, and Recovery in LLM Agents
finding: Loop of Detect, Attribute, Recover, Rerun. A diagnosis agent finds the root cause step, proposes a fix and the task is rerun. An opt-in Error Hub stores failure-diagnosis-repair bundles as reusable debugging memory.
numbers: Who&When: strict agent-and-step attribution 28.8% (qwen3.5-9b) vs 21.7% for the best single-pass baseline. GAIA: repairs 13 of 73 failed tasks in one rerun versus 4-6 for three self-correction baselines; accuracy 55.8% to 63.6%.
limits: Attribution accuracy is still below 30% exact. Single rerun. Open-weight backbones for attribution tests.
agent_relevance: Even good diagnosis is rarely right at the exact step. Do not compile a recovery from a diagnosis alone; G3 says check on something held out.

source: Vuddanti et al. (2026) PALADIN: Self-Correcting Agents to Cure Tool-Failure Cases (ICLR 2026)
finding: Runtime error type is detected, the most similar case in a bank of 55+ failure exemplars is retrieved, and its recovery action is run. The model is LoRA fine-tuned on 50,000+ failure-injected trajectories first.
numbers: Recovery rate 32.76% (ToolBench) to 89.68%; vs strongest baseline CRITIC 76.34% (+13.3). Vanilla agents 23.75% to 89.86%. Keeps 95.2% recovery on unseen tool APIs. Gains significant p<0.01 (bootstrap).
limits: Uses training, not scaffold only. Failures are injected and synthetic. Metrics are the authors' own (RR, TSR, CSR).
agent_relevance: Typed failure plus retrieval of a stored recovery works, which supports a typed impasse table. Training part is outside our scope.

source: Ding (2026) AgentHER: Hindsight Experience Replay for LLM Agent Trajectory Relabeling
finding: Failed trajectories are relabeled as correct demos for an achievable alternative goal and used for fine-tuning. It is learning from failure at trajectory level, offline.
numbers: +7.6 to 11.4% over success-only SFT across four model families on WebArena and ToolBench (task-disjoint test); beats Agent Workflow Memory by +3.0 to 6.2%; 2x sample efficiency; label noise 5.9% to 2.9%; cost $2.98 and 26 minutes for 3,000 trajectories.
limits: Needs training, so not a scaffold-only method. Not scoped to impasses or substates.
agent_relevance: Failed attempts hold usable partial results. A subgoal record could keep the achieved partial result, not just the lesson.

source: Xia et al. (2026) GraSP: Graph-Structured Skill Compositions for LLM Agents
finding: Skills become typed graphs with precondition and effect edges, node-level verification and local repair using five typed operators. A failure repairs only the affected subgraph, not the whole plan.
numbers: ALFWorld ablation (DeepSeek V3.2): ReAct 66.4; all skills no selection 67.1; flat skills 74.9; with DAG compile 78.4; with local repair 79.7; full 80.6. Global replan 77.4. Up to +19 reward over strongest baseline, up to 41% fewer steps; +12.7 over ExpeL on average across 48 cells; precondition failures recovered 84.2%.
limits: Authors' own benchmark suite across eight backbones. Skill library is built, not learned from impasses.
agent_relevance: Local repair beat global replan (79.7 vs 77.4 ALFWorld), a direct number for scoping a subgoal to the failed part. Also 'less is more': 2-3 focused skills beat dumping all.

source: Fan, Lan (2026) From Cognitive Architectures to Language Agents: Mechanism-Level Review
finding: Reviews 10 cognitive architectures, 8 runtimes and 42 modern systems. Concludes the Soar chain (typed impasse, protected substate, typed return, compiled chunk) is not found whole in any current LLM agent.
numbers: Codes PALADIN/AgentDebugX typed recovery as E3/D3, Shepherd reversible branch E2/D3, AgentHER and Reflexion failure learning E3/D4. Names bundle B2 (typed impasse, substate, compilation) as a residual gap.
quote: a learned lesson may lack the conditions that make reuse safe
limits: Preprint, July 2026, no experiments. Codes are the authors' judgments. Bundle B2 is a hypothesis; it fails with misdiagnosis, unsafe compilation, parent-state corruption, or no cut in repeated failure.
agent_relevance: States the failure conditions we must test: misdiagnosis, unsafe compile, parent corruption, no drop in repeat failures. These can be our tests for the subgoal library.

source: Fan, Lan (2026) review: GraSP closes the skill-governance candidate
finding: Closest-baseline screening found GraSP already has multi-skill selection, typed compilation, verification, bounded repair and ReAct fallback. So an LLM-agent skill library with repair exists; the missing piece is the impasse-created isolated substate plus condition-safe compile.
numbers: Five residual bundles remain from the screen; B2 is one.
limits: Authors' own screening, not a systematic search.
agent_relevance: Tells us what is novel for us (impasse-keyed library with stored trigger) versus what is already built.

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan, Griffiths (2024) Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)
finding: Framework paper. Describes Soar: if no action is valid or several tie, an impasse occurs and Soar makes a subgoal, giving hierarchical decomposition. Uses Soar as one source for its decision-cycle design for LLM agents.
numbers: No experiments.
limits: Framework only. Mentions the impasse in one passage.
agent_relevance: Shows the idea is known but the paper does not specify an impasse-driven LLM design; our S6 fills that.

source: Laird, Rosenbloom, Newell (1986) chunking papers and Tambe et al. expensive-chunks work
finding: Original chunking evidence is not read in this angle. The 2026 review and Soar manual cite Laird, Rosenbloom and Newell (1986) as the chunking source. The expensive-chunks (match cost) problem is known from Tambe's work but not opened.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Not opened this session; see angle A and B files for the founding studies.
agent_relevance: Utility problem is the likely boundary: too many chunks slow matching. Check angle A before designing library size limits.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with LLMs
finding: Skill library of verified code programs, retrieved by description for new tasks, with an iterative prompt that adds environment feedback and execution errors. A compiled-skill library in an LLM loop.
numbers: From memory, not verified this session: about 3.3x more unique items, 15.3x faster to wooden tool.
limits: PDF download was corrupt. Numbers are not verified and must be re-checked before use.
agent_relevance: Strongest known LLM skill-library precedent; our check is that skills are stored only after verification.

source: Prasad et al. vs Shinn et al.: whole-trial retry versus subtask retry (within the ADaPT paper)
finding: Head-to-head in one paper: Reflexion (whole-trial reflection) vs ADaPT (retry only the failed subtask). Subtask scope won on all three benchmarks.
numbers: ALFWorld 57.5 vs 71.6; WebShop 35.0 vs 44.0; TextCraft 32.0 vs 52.0 (GPT-3.5).
limits: Run by the ADaPT authors with their own prompts. Not an independent replication.
agent_relevance: Supports scoping a retry to the substate rather than redoing the whole task.

source: GraSP ablation versus global replanning
finding: Replacing local repair with global replanning cost reward in ALFWorld and ScienceWorld. Gap was larger in long tasks.
numbers: GRASP w/ global replan 77.4 ALF / 81.8 SciW vs full 80.6 / 84.9; advantage over ExpeL grows from 6% (10 steps) to 18% (20 steps).
limits: Authors' own ablation; modest gap of about 3 points.
agent_relevance: Scope of a substate matters more as tasks get longer. Another reason to keep the substate narrow.
